newsitem.title: ROMANIA: ROMANIA WOOS ETHNIC GERMANS BACK FROM EMIGRATION.
newsitem.headline: ROMANIA WOOS ETHNIC GERMANS BACK FROM EMIGRATION.

text.p: Romania, keen to boost its chances of early admission to NATO, is trying to mend fences with ethnic Germans who fled the country in the communist era.
"We want to establish good relations with the Saxons and the Swabians who emigrated to Germany," Public Information Minister Radu Boroianu told Reuters on Wednesday.

"They (ethnic Germans) are a bridge linking our countries," said Boroianu, shortly after returning from an unofficial visit to Germany, when met leaders of local groups representing more than 550,000 Saxons and Swabians who emigrated from Romania.
Boroianu, a member of the new centrist coalition government, branded what he called "the criminal cash sale" of ethnic Germans by Romania's ousted communists.

There are no official estimates of the sums which late dictator Nicolae Ceausescu netted from Germany before his 1989 fall and execution, in order to allow the emigration of tens of thousands of ethnic Germans.

The new government and local community leaders now speak of a reversal of that trend, with ethnic Germans expected to return to Romania, drawn by the momentum created by last year's elections, when reformists ended the ex-communists seven-year grip on power.
"Any repatriation would involve the right to housing and jobs," said Boroianu, adding that the government would adopt a "case-by-case" approach to the repatriation issue.

"Things have also improved for us after the elections," Paul Philippi, chairman of the German Democratic Forum told Reuters. "Many ethnic Germans are now interested in returning home. There won't be a wave, but thousands will come back."
Philippi's Forum represents some 100,000 German-speakers still living in Romania after a massive post-communist exodus. Romania had more than 800,000 Germans before World War Two.

Romania's Germans are proud of their 800-year history in Transylvania and the southwest Banat, where Saxon and Swabian settlers built strongholds and fortified villages to defend Christian Europe against Turks and Tartars.

Bucharest is lobbying for Western support to be considered along with Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic, among first candidates for NATO membership when the Alliance announces its first eastward expansion at a July summit in Madrid.
The new Romanian leaders pin their hopes on German Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel's visit to Bucharest at the end of April.
